lesson.title: Tochter: Double Shift Showdown
lesson.subtitle: Words carrying both D→T and GH→CH — discrimination drills

hook.title: The Showdown
hook.content: The double-shift words meet the ghost-map words in one arena. Tochter carries D→T AND gh→ch. dachte (thought) carries TH→D AND gh→ch. Nacht, Licht, acht, Recht, Knecht carry gh→ch alone. The showdown skill: when you see a German t-ch word (Tochter, dachte, Nacht), check BOTH laws — is the t a hardened d (daughter, thought) or was there never a d? Tochter/daughter has both shifts;acht/eight has only the gh. One letter difference in the English twin tells you which laws fired.

footnotes.title: The Three-Way Test
footnotes.content: English night/Nacht: gh→ch only (no d). English daughter/Tochter: d→t AND gh→ch. English thought/dachte: th→d AND gh→ch. Same ch ending, three different English consonant stories. The German ch is constant; the English front tells the tale.

pattern.title: The Showdown Bracket
pattern.content: Match one: Tochter ↔ daughter (D→T + gh→ch) versus Nacht ↔ night (gh→ch only). Match two: dachte ↔ thought (TH→D + gh→ch) versus Licht ↔ light (gh→ch only). Match three: Knecht ↔ knight (gh→ch only — and the social drift!). Match four: acht ↔ eight (gh→ch only). Match five: Recht ↔ right (gh→ch only). The pattern: when the English twin begins with d or th, the German t is doing double duty; when the English twin begins with n, l, e, r, k — the ch is flying solo. Bracket complete.
pattern.linguist_note: The ch of Tochter, Nacht, Licht,acht, Recht, Knecht is phonologically identical — the Ach-Laut after back vowels. The GRAPHIC history differs (t+ch from d+gh, ch from gh), but the sound never changed in German. English silenced one sound; German kept one sound. Simplicity on one shore, complexity on the other.

exercises.prompt: The showdown — match each word with its shift story:
exercises.explanation: Same ch ending — the English front (d, th, or nothing) tells you which laws fired.

options: One: gh → ch (the d never existed here)
exercises.target_answer: One: gh → ch (the d never existed here)
exercises.explanation: Both start with k — no dental involved. Only the guttural changed (or rather, only English silenced it). The night sky again: der Mond, der Stern — and hell (bright) is what the moon makes of the dark.

exercises.prompt: Which pair runs THREE laws including th→d and gh→ch?
exercises.explanation: th→d, the vowel drift, gh→ch — thought/dachte is the most heavily shifted common pair in the language. (selbst stays bare — ich selbst — the v→b law from the hunt.)

exercises.prompt: What English word is the twin of 'Tochter'?
exercises.explanation: The double-shift flagship — d hardened AND the guttural survived, in one family word.

exercises.prompt: Assemble: 'The daughter thought at night' (mixed past!)
exercises.target_answer: Die Tochter dachte in der Nacht
exercises.meaning: Die Tochter dachte in der Nacht = The daughter thought at night

vocab_hints.note: in + dative (location in time) — der Nacht is the feminine dative

exercises.explanation: Three gh→ch/t-ch words in one sentence — Tochter (double), dachte (triple), Nacht (single). The showdown, staged. Die Nichte (the niece) belongs to the Tochter family set — kin words for the double-shift daughter.

summary.outcome: Discriminate single-shift ghost words from double-shift twins at speed.

use_example.german: Die Tochter dachte in der Nacht.

summary.takeaway: The ch ending is constant — the English front (d, th, or nothing) reports how many laws fired.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Next: sagen & gestern — the Y→G twins close the Atlas families for good.

twist.target_answer: Die Tochter dachte in der Nacht

tochter.context_phrase: Meine Tochter lernt in der Schule.
tochter.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and gh → ch.

nacht.context_phrase: In der Nacht ist es hier sehr ruhig.
nacht.context_translation: At night it is very quiet here.

knecht.context_phrase: Der Knecht arbeitet auf dem Hof.
knecht.context_translation: The farmhand works on the estate.
knecht.etymology_derivation: gh → ch (knight ↔ Knecht). In English it elevated to noble warrior; in German it remained farm servant.

denken.etymology_derivation: TH → D hardening. Shares the exact vowel-shift relationship with "danken" that English has in "think" and "thank" (a thank is a good thought).

mitternacht.etymology_derivation: Mitter + Nacht — inherited from Proto-Germanic *midjanahts, the very same middle-night compound as English midnight. [wiktionary]

nichte.context_translation: My niece is playing in the garden.
nichte.etymology_derivation: This form replaced obsolete Niftel in the 17th century; English niece is a Latin loan of the same kinship root. [wiktionary]

selbst.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic *selbaz; the page lists English self as the direct cognate — the f closing to b in German plus an excrescent t. [wiktionary]

hell.etymology_derivation: Proto-Germanic *halliz 'resounding'; English bright/light is not cognate — hell is akin to English hall. [wiktionary]

mond.context_phrase: Der Mond ist heute Nacht hell.
mond.etymology_derivation: Proto-West Germanic *mānō — the same ancient moon-word as English moon. [wiktionary]

stern.context_phrase: Ich sehe einen Stern am Himmel.
stern.context_translation: I see a star in the sky.
stern.etymology_derivation: Old High German sterno — cognate with English star. [wiktionary]

treu.context_phrase: Ein treuer Freund ist viel wert.
treu.context_translation: A faithful friend is worth a lot.

taub.context_phrase: Er ist auf einem Ohr taub.
taub.context_translation: He is deaf in one ear.
taub.etymology_derivation: Double shift: d → t and f/v → b.

topf.context_translation: The soup is cooking in the pot.
topf.etymology_derivation: From Proto-Germanic duppaz, meaning hollow thing; the listed English cognate is dop, the diamond-cutter's cup, and the same PIE hollow root dewb gives English deep, with d becoming t in High German. [wiktionary]

haustier.context_phrase: Ein Hund ist ein beliebtes Haustier.
haustier.context_translation: A dog is a popular pet.
haustier.etymology_derivation: A compound of Haus and Tier, both direct cognates: house and deer, since Tier originally meant any animal. [wiktionary]

u-bahn.context_phrase: Ich nehme die U-Bahn zur Arbeit.
u-bahn.context_translation: I take the underground to work.
u-bahn.etymology_derivation: Short for Untergrundbahn, the underground railway: unter (under), Grund (ground, with the English d become German t), Bahn (railway). [wiktionary]

regenmantel.etymology_derivation: Regen + Mantel — the compound calque of raincoat; Regen is the twin of rain (y → g). [wiktionary]

th_to_d.name: The Dental Shift (TH → D)
th_to_d.historical_linguistics: Every single original Germanic "th" sound systematically shifted to "d" in High German, while English kept the ancient "th".
th_to_d.philological_note: Around 500–700 AD in the High German Consonant Shift, dental fricatives hardened into voiced dental stops.

d_to_t.name: The Stop Shift (D → T)
d_to_t.historical_linguistics: Where English kept Germanic "d", High German hardened it into "t".
d_to_t.philological_note: Voiced stops became voiceless. Explains pairs like day ↔ Tag, door ↔ Tür, and drink ↔ trinken.
d_to_t.literature_source: Complementary to the TH → D shift: as TH took over D, original D shifted to T in High German.

p_to_pf_f.name: The Labial Shift (P → PF / F)
p_to_pf_f.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /p/ shifted to the affricate "pf" at the beginning of words, and to "f" or "ff" after vowels.
p_to_pf_f.philological_note: Explains apple ↔ Apfel, pepper ↔ Pfeffer, hope ↔ hoffen, and sleep ↔ schlafen.

t_to_s_ss_z.name: The Sibilant Shift (T → S / SS / Z)
t_to_s_ss_z.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /t/ shifted to sibilant "s/ss/ß" after vowels, and to "z" (/ts/) at the beginning of words.
t_to_s_ss_z.philological_note: Reveals water ↔ Wasser, eat ↔ essen, better ↔ besser, two ↔ zwei, and to ↔ zu.
t_to_s_ss_z.literature_source: Walter Skeat - Primary dental affrication and spirantization

k_to_ch.name: The Velar Shift (K → CH)
k_to_ch.historical_linguistics: Proto-Germanic /k/ softened to the fricative "ch" in medial and final positions.
k_to_ch.philological_note: The Ach-Laut [x] occurs after a, o, u; the Ich-Laut [ç] occurs after e, i, ä, ö, ü.

v_to_b.name: The Bilabial Shift (V / F → B)
v_to_b.historical_linguistics: Intervocalic /v/ and /f/ in English regularly correspond to voiced /b/ in German.
v_to_b.philological_note: Explains give ↔ geben, live ↔ leben, love ↔ lieben, over ↔ über, and seven ↔ sieben.
v_to_b.literature_source: Proto-Germanic bilabial spirant closing to stop in High German

y_gh_to_g_ch.name: The Palatal & Guttural Link (Y → G & GH → CH)
y_gh_to_g_ch.historical_linguistics: English vocalized palatal "g" into "y" (say, day, yesterday) and silenced "gh" (night, laugh, light). German preserved them as "g" or "ch".
y_gh_to_g_ch.philological_note: Explains why English spelling has silent 'gh' letters — they were original German-like gutturals!

latin_ieren.name: The Latin / Romance Layer (-ate / -ize → -ieren)
latin_ieren.phonetic_rule: English verbs ending in -ate, -ize, -ify, -ish ➔ German verbs ending in -ieren
latin_ieren.historical_linguistics: English verbs derived from Latin or French directly map to German verbs ending in -ieren.
latin_ieren.philological_note: Past participles of -ieren verbs never take the "ge-" prefix (studieren → studiert).
latin_ieren.literature_source: Middle High German productive loan suffix from Old French -ier

strong_verbs_ablaut.name: The 7 Strong Verb Classes (Ablaut)
strong_verbs_ablaut.phonetic_rule: English irregular strong verbs with internal vowel changes ➔ German strong verbs following the exact same Ablautreihe
strong_verbs_ablaut.historical_linguistics: Shared 7 Proto-Germanic verb classes where tenses are formed by shifting root vowels.
